text: You're building a custom table to track vendor risk assessments, and your manager hands you a one-sentence requirement: Risk Level needs to be one of a fixed set of options, Low, Medium, High, or Critical, and every assessment record needs one set before it can be saved. Nothing here requires a screenshot — every decision below is something you'd reason through out loud, the same way you'd justify it in a real design review.

First, the field type. A fixed set of options rules out String immediately — free text would let someone type something inconsistent, like kinda high, defeating the entire point of a fixed set. It also rules out Boolean, since there are four states here, not two. That's exactly what Choice exists for: a value that must come from a predefined list, enforced by the platform instead of hoped for. So on the new field's dictionary entry, you set Type equals Choice, which is also what makes a sys_choice list relevant to this field at all.

With Type set to Choice, you add four rows to sys_choice, one per value, each tied to your new table and the risk_level field name: Low, Medium, High, and Critical, numbered one through four in increasing severity, with sequence numbers controlling display order. Numeric values are worth choosing deliberately here — if a future report ever needs to filter High and above, a numeric value sorts correctly by severity, where plain text would sort alphabetically and land completely out of order.

The requirement also says every record needs a value set before it can save — that's not a suggestion, it's a hard save-time rule, and it's exactly what the Mandatory flag from Lesson 15 enforces. Check that flag on the risk_level dictionary entry and save it, and from that moment on, every form built against this table refuses to save a blank Risk Level, with no code written and no separate validation rule required anywhere.

Three decisions, start to finish: you picked Choice over String or Boolean because the requirement demanded a fixed set, you defined that set as ordered, numerically-valued sys_choice rows instead of leaving it to free text, and you enforced the save-time rule with Mandatory instead of just hoping it would work out. Type, values, constraints — that sequence applies to every field you'll ever add, to any table. Next up, Chapter Five: Form Layout and Form Design.
